# ======================================================
# 🔄 7. Creating a New Variable
# ======================================================

It's important to understand how to manipulate the variables in your data frame. Consider, again, the `education` variable.

* What type of variable is `education`? Let's use `str()` to check how it's coded in our data frame.

```{webr-r}
str(data$education)
```

Based on this, we see that `education` is a character variable — we know that because `str()` labels it **`chr`** right at the start of the output.

`str()` uses a short abbreviation for every variable type, and it's worth being able to recognize the common ones at a glance:

| Abbreviation | Type | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `chr` | character (text/string) | `education`, `gender` |
| `int` | integer (whole numbers) | `id`, `year` |
| `num` | numeric (double — can hold decimals) | `age`, `hrlctree` |
| `logi` | logical (`TRUE`/`FALSE`) | rare in survey data, but common after a comparison like `age > 65` |
| `Factor` | factor (categorical, with defined levels) | not currently used in this dataset — R reads categories in as `chr` by default, but some analyses expect `Factor` instead |

## Creating a numeric version of the education variable

Right now, `education` is a character variable — useful for reading and for `table()`, but not for most quantitative work. **Regression models, correlations, and most statistical functions in R need numeric input** — they can't compute something like a mean, a correlation coefficient, or a regression slope on the text strings `"< Bachelor's"` and `"Bachelor's degree or higher"`. To use education status as a predictor or outcome in that kind of analysis later in the course, we first need a consistently coded numeric (here, binary 0/1) version. Let's do this now, using base R's `ifelse()`:

::: {.callout-note}
**A note for later in the course:** if you only ever plan to use `education` as an *explanatory* variable (a predictor) in a regression model — not as the outcome — converting it to a numeric 0/1 variable isn't your only option. R's regression functions (like `lm()` and `glm()`) can also take a **factor** variable directly as a predictor, and will automatically create the 0/1 coding behind the scenes (this is called "dummy coding"). For a variable with just two categories like this one, numeric 0/1 and factor give you the same result either way. The numeric approach shown here is worth learning first because it makes that dummy-coding step explicit rather than hidden — but once you're comfortable with what's happening, `factor()` is often the more natural choice for a categorical predictor, especially one with more than two levels.
:::

```{webr-r}
data$num_education <- ifelse(data$education == "< Bachelor's", 0, 1)
```

**What happened here?** This line creates a new variable called `num_education`, a numeric version of `education`, using `ifelse()`:

* The code checks each value of `education`.
* If the value is `"< Bachelor's"` (less than a bachelor's degree), `num_education` is set to `0`.
* For all other values (presumably at least a bachelor's degree), `num_education` is set to `1`.

So this line recodes a categorical `education` variable into a binary (0/1) numeric variable, where:

* `0` = less than a bachelor's degree
* `1` = bachelor's degree or higher

**Note:** in R there are lots of ways to do the same thing. Another way to recode this variable is with the `dplyr` package (loaded as part of `tidyverse`) instead of base R's `ifelse()`.

Quick reminder of the syntax before you try it: `mutate()` adds (or changes) a column in a data frame, and `if_else()` works like `ifelse()` — a condition, then the value to use when it's `TRUE`, then the value to use when it's `FALSE`. Put together, the general pattern looks like:

```r
data <- data %>%
  mutate(new_column_name = if_else(some_condition, value_if_true, value_if_false))
```

::: {.callout-tip title="🧠 Your Turn"}
`dplyr`'s equivalent of `ifelse()` is `if_else()`, typically used inside `mutate()`. Try rewriting the `num_education` recode above using `data %>% mutate(...)` and `if_else()` instead of base R. Call the new column `num_education2` so you can compare it to the original.
:::

```{webr-r}
# Your code here — recreate num_education using mutate() + if_else(), call it num_education2

```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="💡 Solution — click to reveal"}
```{webr-r}
data <- data %>%
  mutate(num_education2 = if_else(education == "< Bachelor's", 0, 1))
```
:::

Verify that the coding of the new variable worked as we wanted, by creating a two-by-two table looking at the distribution of the numeric education variable against the character one:

```{webr-r}
table(data$num_education, data$education)
```

# ======================================================
# 📝 8. Merging Data with External Information
# ======================================================

A lot of times in environmental epidemiology, we have additional environmental information that we want to link into our data. Examples include:

* Air pollution data
* Housing data
* Tract-level sociodemographic composition variables
* Green space data
* Crime data

You can probably think of additional types of data we might want to link in.

Why would we want to do this? Here's a concrete example: if we're interested in studying the association between residential air pollution exposure and asthma diagnosis, our survey data alone won't have an air pollution measurement for each participant — so we'd want to link in a separate data source that does have it, matched to where each participant lives.

We can do this by **merging** a second data frame — which has the environmental information of interest — into our primary data frame, by combining them using a common variable or variables.

* Often, we use information about participants' neighborhoods (e.g., census tracts) to merge in environmental data. A **census tract** is a small, relatively permanent geographic area defined by the U.S. Census Bureau — roughly neighborhood-sized, typically a few thousand residents — that's commonly used in public health research as a proxy for someone's local environment, since exact addresses usually aren't available (or shared) for privacy reasons.

Let's do that now.

******

## Load another dataset

You'll find an additional data frame, which contains neighborhood-level (tract-level) data on **NDVI** (greenness), called `PHL_NDVI_summer_annual.csv`. (For the other tract-level environmental and sociodemographic variables already in `data` — like `hrlctree` or `pov_allage` — see the [Data Codebook](codebook.qmd).)

This data frame shows the median value of the summertime NDVI value for each census tract in Philadelphia — that is, how green each census tract is. NDVI stands for Normalized Difference Vegetation Index. *NDVI ranges in value from -1 to 1.*

* Negative values represent water.
* Values close to 1 mean dense vegetation.
* Values close to 0 mean a lack of vegetation (there might instead be lots of concrete).

[This page](https://gisgeography.com/ndvi-normalized-difference-vegetation-index/) tells us a bit more about NDVI.

Let's read in that data (again, in the browser we first fetch it from the web; in RStudio you'd just need it saved in your `data_raw/` folder):

```{webr-r}
#| autorun: true

download.file(paste0(data_base_url, "PHL_NDVI_summer_annual.csv"), file.path("data_raw", "PHL_NDVI_summer_annual.csv"))

PHL_NDVI_summer_annual <- read.csv(file.path("data_raw", "PHL_NDVI_summer_annual.csv"))
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## 💻 In your RStudio script

The chunk above fetches the NDVI file from the web for the browser. **In your own RStudio script**, with `PHL_NDVI_summer_annual.csv` already in your `data_raw/` folder, all you need is:

```r
PHL_NDVI_summer_annual <- read.csv(file.path("data_raw", "PHL_NDVI_summer_annual.csv"))
```
:::

Inspect the dataset using the `names`, `str`, and `head` functions. Do you remember what each of these shows you?

```{webr-r}
names(PHL_NDVI_summer_annual)
str(PHL_NDVI_summer_annual)
head(PHL_NDVI_summer_annual)
```

**Questions:**

* How many observations (rows) are in the NDVI data frame?
* What are the names of the variables (columns) in this data frame?
* What seems to be the unique identifier in the NDVI data frame?

******

## Summarize the NDVI values across Philadelphia

Using our Philadelphia tract-level data frame, let's look at the distribution of NDVI across the city of Philadelphia.

* What is the minimum NDVI value? What does this tell you?
* What's the median? What's the max?

```{webr-r}
summary(PHL_NDVI_summer_annual$X2015_NDVI)
```

* But we want to know how green the neighborhoods of our study participants are.
* To do so, we're going to link the NDVI data frame to our primary data frame using a common variable found in both.

The common variable is called **geoid10**. In our class data frame, `geoid10` refers to the census tract in which the study participant lives. In the NDVI data frame, `GEOID10` refers to each unique Philadelphia census tract.

In order for the merge/linkage to work, both variables have to be in the **same format** (both character, or both numeric, etc.). Let's check on this now.

```{webr-r}
str(data$geoid10)
str(PHL_NDVI_summer_annual$GEOID10)
```

Notice these **don't match**: `data$geoid10` shows up as `chr`, because we deliberately converted it back in Section 5 of Part 2, and again in the setup chunk at the top of this page (it's a label, not a quantity, remember?) — but `PHL_NDVI_summer_annual$GEOID10` is freshly read in from its own file and is still `num`. This is exactly the situation the earlier conversion was setting up: without it, both would have looked numeric and matched by coincidence, hiding the fact that ID columns need this treatment at all. Since they don't match now, let's convert `GEOID10` to character too:

```{webr-r}
PHL_NDVI_summer_annual$GEOID10 <- as.character(PHL_NDVI_summer_annual$GEOID10)
```

(Re-running `data$geoid10 <- as.character(data$geoid10)` here as well wouldn't hurt anything — converting an already-character column to character is a harmless no-op — but it's only *necessary* for the one that's still numeric.)

Now let's merge the datasets, using a left join:

```{webr-r}
data2 <- merge(data, PHL_NDVI_summer_annual, by.x = 'geoid10', by.y = 'GEOID10', all.x = TRUE)
```

Now the data frame called `data2` should have all of our original variables, plus the variables from the NDVI data frame.

As a check, think about how many variables were in each separate data frame.

* How many rows are in `data2`?

We're specifically checking this because a left join (`all.x = TRUE`) is supposed to keep **every** row from `data` — one row per participant, no more and no fewer — while just adding columns from `PHL_NDVI_summer_annual` onto each one. If the row count in `data2` doesn't match the row count in `data` (2,000), that's a red flag: it would mean the merge either dropped some participants, or duplicated some (which happens if the NDVI file accidentally has more than one row per `geoid10` — each extra match creates an extra output row). Checking `nrow()` before and after any merge is one of the simplest, most important habits for confirming a merge did what you expected.

```{webr-r}
num_rows <- nrow(data2)

print(num_rows)
```

Or we can use `dim()`, which shows us rows and columns:

```{webr-r}
dim(data2)
```

We can also look at the names of the variables in the merged data frame — is everything in there?

```{webr-r}
names(data2)
```

It's also helpful to look at the top rows of the merged data frame, to be sure we don't have a bunch of missing values (coded `NA`) — if we see missings in the NDVI variables, that likely means something went wrong with our merge!

```{webr-r}
head(data2)
```

We can also do some logic checks to be sure everything checks out.

::: {.callout-tip title="🧠 Your Turn"}
Do participants living in the identical census tract get assigned the **same** NDVI value? Write code to check this — for example, group `data2` by `geoid10` and count the number of *distinct* `X2015_NDVI` values within each tract. If the merge worked correctly, every tract should have exactly 1 distinct NDVI value.

**Why should that be true?** `X2015_NDVI` is a *tract-level* measurement — it describes the neighborhood, not the individual person. A left join doesn't create new NDVI values; it just looks up the one value that belongs to each participant's `geoid10` and copies it onto every row that matches. So everyone sharing a tract should end up with the identical copied value. If any tract shows more than one distinct value, something's wrong — most likely a formatting issue (like the one we just fixed) that caused some participants to match the wrong row, or a duplicate tract entry in the NDVI file itself.

(Hint: `dplyr`'s `group_by()`, `summarize()`, and `n_distinct()` are useful here.)
:::

```{webr-r}
# Your code here — check that every geoid10 tract has exactly one unique NDVI value

```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="💡 Solution — click to reveal"}
```{webr-r}
data2 %>%
  group_by(geoid10) %>%
  summarize(n_unique_ndvi = n_distinct(X2015_NDVI)) %>%
  count(n_unique_ndvi)
```
**What this output is telling you:** the `summarize()` step produces one row per tract, giving the number of distinct NDVI values found within it (`n_unique_ndvi`) — then `count(n_unique_ndvi)` collapses *that* down into a small frequency table, showing how many tracts (`n`) had each possible value of `n_unique_ndvi`. What you're looking for is a **single row**: `n_unique_ndvi = 1`, with `n` equal to the total number of tracts (384) — meaning every tract, without exception, has exactly one NDVI value. If you instead saw a second row (e.g., `n_unique_ndvi = 2` with some nonzero `n`), that would tell you exactly how many tracts have the problem, which is your starting point for troubleshooting.
:::

Assuming everything looks OK, let's move on. If not, we'd need to do some troubleshooting!

# ======================================================
# 📂 9. Saving Your Processed Data
# ======================================================

Currently, our new data frame just lives in our R environment (or, on this page, in your browser's temporary in-browser R session). Once we close R (or this browser tab), we lose our changes unless we save them. We can either rerun this code again, or save our new data frame with any changes we made. Let's do this now.

**Note:** it's good practice to save your data frame using a **new** name, and — per this course's project convention — into `data_processed/`, not `data_raw/`. That way `data_raw/class_data_raw.csv` stays untouched as your original source, and anyone (including you, later) can tell at a glance that `data_processed/` files were generated by a script rather than hand-edited.

Why does that separation matter so much? Think about reproducibility (recall this from Week 1): the whole point of the `data_raw/` → script → `data_processed/` pattern is that your **script**, not a person clicking around in a spreadsheet, is the record of every transformation applied to the data. If `class_data_raw.csv` ever got hand-edited directly, there would be no way to tell what changed or why — the original data would effectively be lost, and nobody (including future you) could regenerate it from scratch. Keeping `data_raw/` untouched means you can always delete `data_processed/` entirely and rebuild it by just re-running your script — which is exactly what "reproducible" means in practice.

::: {.callout-tip}
## 💻 In your RStudio script

This is the line to use in your own script to save the processed dataset. The `data_processed/` folder already exists in your `EOH635_project` from the setup assignment:

```r
write.csv(data2, file.path("data_processed", "class_data_processed.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
```

This saves `class_data_processed.csv` into `data_processed/` inside your project, where it will persist between sessions.
:::

You can also run the chunk below in the browser to see how it works — but note that in the browser the file is only saved temporarily and disappears when you close the tab. **To actually save this file permanently to your hard drive, run the single line shown in the green "In your RStudio script" box just above, inside RStudio** — with `data2` in your R environment and `data_processed/` already existing in your `EOH635_project`, that `write.csv(...)` line writes the file to your computer's disk, where it will still be there the next time you open RStudio.

```{webr-r}
dir.create("data_processed", showWarnings = FALSE)

# Save dataset
write.csv(data2, file.path("data_processed", "class_data_processed.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
```

# ======================================================
# 🚀 10. Quick-Start Script for Your Own Project
# ======================================================

This script covers only the **data preparation** work we did in this lesson — reading in the NDVI data, merging it with our primary dataset, and recoding the `education` variable. It's not a full analysis; think of it as getting your dataset ready for one. Everything above walked through each of those steps one at a time, with the browser-only fetching code mixed in. Below is everything put together as a **single clean script** — this is what actually goes in your `.R` or `.qmd` file inside `EOH635_project/scripts/`, running on your own computer with `class_data_raw.csv` and `PHL_NDVI_summer_annual.csv` already sitting in `data_raw/`.

::: {.callout-tip}
## 💻 In your RStudio script

Copy the whole block below into a new script in RStudio to get started on your own computer. There's no downloading step here — R just reads the files straight from your `data_raw/` folder.

```r
# ---- Setup ----
library(tidyverse)

# ---- Read in your data ----
data <- read.csv(file.path("data_raw", "class_data_raw.csv"))
PHL_NDVI_summer_annual <- read.csv(file.path("data_raw", "PHL_NDVI_summer_annual.csv"))

# ---- Take a first look ----
head(data)
str(data)
dim(data)
summary(data)

# ---- Recode education into a numeric 0/1 variable ----
data <- data %>%
  mutate(num_education = if_else(education == "< Bachelor's", 0, 1))

# ---- Match variable types before merging ----
data$geoid10 <- as.character(data$geoid10)
PHL_NDVI_summer_annual$GEOID10 <- as.character(PHL_NDVI_summer_annual$GEOID10)

# ---- Merge in the NDVI (greenness) data ----
data2 <- merge(data, PHL_NDVI_summer_annual,
                by.x = "geoid10", by.y = "GEOID10", all.x = TRUE)

# ---- Check that the merge worked ----
dim(data2)
head(data2)

# ---- Save your processed dataset ----
write.csv(data2, file.path("data_processed", "class_data_processed.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
```
:::
